pairs.source_text: ubi autem commemoravi legisse me quosdam libros platonicorum, quos Victorinus, quondam rhetor urbis Romae, quem christianum defunctum esse audieram, in latinam linguam transtulisset, gratulatus est mihi quod non in aliorum philosophorum scripta incidissem plena fallaciarum et deceptionum secundum elementa huius mundi.
pairs.question: Quis libros platonicorum, quos Augustinus legerat, in latinam linguam transtulit?
pairs.question_en: Who translated into Latin the books of the Platonists that Augustine had read?
pairs.derivation: Augustine recounts to Simplicianus that he had read certain Platonist books which Victorinus, once a rhetor of the city of Rome, had translated into Latin. Anchored to the libri platonicorum + Latin; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'quos Victorinus ... in latinam linguam transtulisset.' Closed-book: Marius Victorinus's Latin renderings of the Neoplatonists are a well-known fact of intellectual history.

pairs.source_text: doctor tot nobilium senatorum, qui etiam ob insigne praeclari magisterii, quod cives huius mundi eximium putant, statuam Romano foro meruerat et acceperat.
pairs.question: In quo loco Victorinus rhetor, ob praeclarum magisterium, statuam meruit et accepit?
pairs.question_en: In what place did Victorinus the rhetor earn and receive a statue, on account of his distinguished teaching?
pairs.derivation: Victorinus, teacher of many noble senators, earned and received a statue in the Roman forum for his eminent teaching of rhetoric. Anchored to Victorinus the rhetor; place answer supported verbatim by 'statuam Romano foro meruerat et acceperat.' Closed-book biographical detail (his statue in the forum is a famous mark of his standing as rhetor at Rome).

pairs.source_text: sed ubi mihi homo tuus Simplicianus de Victorino ista narravit, exarsi ad imitandum: ad hoc enim et ille narraverat.
pairs.question: Quis Augustino de conversione Victorini rhetoris narravit?
pairs.question_en: Who recounted to Augustine the conversion of Victorinus the rhetor?
pairs.derivation: It was Simplicianus who told Augustine the story of Victorinus's conversion, precisely to spur him to imitate it. Anchored to Augustine + Victorinus; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'Simplicianus de Victorino ista narravit.' Closed-book (Simplicianus, later bishop of Milan, is a recognized figure in the conversion narrative).

pairs.source_text: posteaquam vero et illud addidit, quod imperatoris Iuliani temporibus lege data prohibiti sunt christiani docere litteraturam et oratoriam. quam legem ille amplexus, loquacem scholam deserere maluit.
pairs.question: Cuius imperatoris temporibus christiani lege data docere litteraturam et oratoriam prohibiti sunt?
pairs.question_en: In which emperor's reign were Christians forbidden by a law to teach literature and rhetoric?
pairs.derivation: Augustine reports that under the emperor Julian a law forbade Christians to teach literature and rhetoric, a law Victorinus embraced by leaving his school. Anchored to the school-teaching ban; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'imperatoris Iuliani temporibus lege data prohibiti sunt christiani docere litteraturam et oratoriam.' Closed-book (Julian's edict on teachers, AD 362, is established Roman history).

pairs.source_text: cui ego cum indicassem illis me scripturis curam maximam impendere, ortus est sermo ipso narrante de Antonio Aegyptio monacho, cuius nomen excellenter clarebat apud servos tuos, nos autem usque in illam horam latebat.
pairs.question: Quis, cum in domum Augustini et Alypii venisset, eis de Antonio Aegyptio monacho narravit?
pairs.question_en: Who, having come to the house of Augustine and Alypius, told them about Antony the Egyptian monk?
pairs.derivation: The teller ('ipso narrante') is Ponticianus, named at the opening of 8.6.14 ('ad nos domum venit ad me et Alypium Ponticianus quidam ... praeclare in palatio militans'). Anchored to Augustine + Alypius + Antony; single-name answer. Closed-book: Ponticianus's visit is the famous trigger of Augustine's conversion.

pairs.source_text: ortus est sermo ipso narrante de Antonio Aegyptio monacho, cuius nomen excellenter clarebat apud servos tuos, nos autem usque in illam horam latebat.
pairs.question: Quo nomine appellatur monachus Aegyptius de quo Ponticianus apud Augustinum narravit?
pairs.question_en: By what name is the Egyptian monk called about whom Ponticianus spoke at Augustine's house?
pairs.derivation: Ponticianus's conversation turned to Antony, the Egyptian monk. Anchored to Ponticianus + Egyptian monk; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'de Antonio Aegyptio monacho.' Closed-book (Antony of Egypt is among the most famous of the early monks).

pairs.source_text: sed illos vagabundos inruisse in quandam casam ubi habitabant quidam servi tui spiritu pauperes, qualium est regnum caelorum, et invenisse ibi codicem in quo scripta erat vita Antonii. quam legere coepit unus eorum et mirari et accendi, et inter legendum meditari arripere talem vitam et relicta militia saeculari servire tibi. erant autem ex eis quos dicunt agentes in rebus.
pairs.question: Cuius vita scripta erat in codice quem agentes in rebus, Ponticiani contubernales, reppererunt, quo lecto militiam saecularem reliquerunt?
pairs.question_en: Whose life was written in the codex that the agentes in rebus, Ponticianus's companions, found, and which, once read, made them abandon their worldly service?
pairs.derivation: Two of Ponticianus's fellow court officials ('agentes in rebus') found in a cottage a codex containing the Life of Antony, and reading it abandoned their imperial careers. Anchored to the officials + the codex; answer supported verbatim by 'codicem in quo scripta erat vita Antonii.' Closed-book (the role of Athanasius's Vita Antonii in these conversions is a famous episode).

pairs.source_text: et ecce audio vocem de vicina domo cum cantu dicentis et crebro repetentis, quasi pueri an puellae, nescio: 'tolle lege, tolle lege.'
pairs.question: Quae verba Augustinus, in horto sedens, a voce quasi pueri vel puellae de vicina domo crebro repeti audivit?
pairs.question_en: What words did Augustine, sitting in the garden, hear repeated again and again by a voice as of a boy or girl from a neighboring house?
pairs.derivation: The famous chant that prompted Augustine to open the apostle's codex. Anchored to Augustine + the garden scene; the quoted words are supported verbatim by "'tolle lege, tolle lege.'" Closed-book (one of the most famous moments in the Confessions) and translatable ('take up and read').

pairs.source_text: et forte supra mensam lusoriam quae ante nos erat attendit codicem. tulit, aperuit, invenit apostolum Paulum, inopinate sane: putaverat enim aliquid de libris quorum professio me conterebat.
pairs.question: Cuius apostoli scripta continebat codex, quem Ponticianus in domo Augustini aperuit et quem Augustinus postea in horto arripuit ac legit?
pairs.question_en: Whose apostolic writings did the codex contain, which Ponticianus opened in Augustine's house and which Augustine afterward seized and read in the garden?
pairs.derivation: The codex on the gaming table that Ponticianus opened proved to contain 'apostolum Paulum'; it is the same 'codicem apostoli' Augustine seized and read at his conversion (8.12.29, Rom. 13:13-14). Anchored to Augustine; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'invenit apostolum Paulum.' Closed-book (Augustine's conversion reading of Paul is famous).

pairs.source_text: itaque concitus redii in eum locum ubi sedebat Alypius: ibi enim posueram codicem apostoli cum inde surrexeram. arripui, aperui, et legi in silentio capitulum quo primum coniecti sunt oculi mei.
pairs.question: Quis amicus una cum Augustino in horto sedebat quo tempore, codice apostoli arripto, ad fidem conversus est?
pairs.question_en: Which friend was sitting with Augustine in the garden at the time when, having seized the apostle's codex, he was converted to the faith?
pairs.derivation: Alypius was beside Augustine throughout the garden scene ('Alypius affixus lateri meo' 8.11.27; 'ubi sedebat Alypius' 8.12.29; 'indicavi Alypio' 8.12.30) and converted with him. Anchored to Augustine + the garden conversion; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'redii in eum locum ubi sedebat Alypius.' Closed-book (Alypius is Augustine's well-known companion).
